newsitem.title: USA: Gore-Chernomyrdin talks on NATO, space, summit.
newsitem.headline: Gore-Chernomyrdin talks on NATO, space, summit.

text.p: Russian fears about NATO, U.S. jitters about the global space station and plans for a presidential summit will be prime topics this week in talks between Vice President Al Gore and Russia's prime minister.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin arrived on Wednesday for the latest in a series of discussions with Gore, but this time the talks have added weight: the two Number Twos have been charged with setting an agenda -- as well as a time and place -- for a summit between President Bill Clinton and recuperating Russian President Boris Yeltsin.

The Gore-Chernomyrdin discussions, which begin on Thursday, will likely be coloured by vehement concerns voiced by Chernomyrdin about NATO's plans to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to become members in the alliance.

"I'm worried about Russia," Chernomyrdin said in an interview published on Tuesday in the Washington Post. The West "wants us to explain to our people that there is nothing to fear. How can we explain this? Nobody is going to listen to any explanations ... Developments in Russia could take an ominous turn."

Faced with Chernomyrdin's stated anxiety that NATO expansion into central Europe could undermine Yeltsin's government and give impetus to ultranationalists, U.S. officials have been talking soothingly.

"Our course of action (on NATO expansion) has been determined," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said before Chernomyrdin's arrival. "The point is to make it work and to make it work for all nations, including the Russian Federation."
"Russia can have, we believe should have, a very substantive role in creating a security structure in Europe," another senior U.S. official said on the basis of anonymity.

But Americans are concerned about another facet of the U.S.-Russian relationship: the Russian space agency's ability to make good on commitments to the $40 billion international space station project.

"We have no doubts about their science and engineering proficiency," one U.S. official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. "Where we have concerns relates to adequate funding on the Russian side."

Construction of the space station, which is led by the United States and includes contributions from Russia, Japan, Europe and Canada, had been due to get under way in November, but a crucial Russian component is months behind schedule, hampered by the Russian space agency's money problems.

There have been rumbles on Captol Hill suggesting Russia should withdraw as a full partner in the project if it cannot meet its obligations. Russia maintains it has budgeted all the cash it needs to satisfy its requirements for the station.
Both sides have said the Gore-Chernomyrdin meeting is the appropriate forum to thrash out these difficulties.

Chernomyrdin's schedule includes meetings with World Bank President James Wolfensohn and congressional leaders, in addition to the official meeting with Gore at the State Department on Thursday and Friday.
Gore and Chernomyrdin will travel to Chicago on Saturday.

The so-called Gore-Chernomyrdin Commission, which has met every six months since 1993, was designed to do away with barriers left over from the Cold War era by having Cabinet-level committees work out accords on economic and technological issues.
It has evolved into a key channel for diplomatic business between Washington and Moscow, especially in light of the health problems that have recently sidelined Yeltsin.
U.S. officials point to some 150 nuts-and-bolts agreements facilitated by the commission, notably moves to reassure U.S. investors about Russian oil and gas ventures.
